text:
B: Hello.
A: Hi. Erm, I'm Kirsty.
B: Neil. Halifax.
A: Burnley.
B: Not far, then. Over the tops.
A: Yeah. I've been to Hebden Bridge a few times on the bus. Is that near you?
B: Near enough. I was working there last week, on a chapel.
A: Oh. What do you do?
B: Stonemason. Restoration work. You?
A: Erm, nothing at the minute. I was in a factory. I got made redundant.
B: Right. Rotten luck.
A: Yeah.
B: You had a drawing on your wall in that photo. A lock, was it?
A: Yeah. Mine. The one near me on the canal.
B: Thought it might be. You'd got the coping stones right. Most people draw them like bricks.
A: Oh. Thanks. I sat on the wall and did it, 'cause the photo made them look flat. You had one as well, a window.
B: Church window. St John's, the Minster. I did that when we were doing the tracery on the south side. Drawing's half the job, really. You can't carve owt you haven't drawn first.
A: Is it hard, carving?
B: It's slow. You can't put stone back once it's off. So you think a lot before you hit it. Er, I like that, though. You can't rush it, and nobody can make you.
A: That sounds nice, actually. Nobody rushing you.
B: It is, mostly. Till a project manager turns up.
A: Do you find old things in them? The buildings?
B: Sometimes. Found a mason's mark last month on a mill in Sowerby Bridge. Little arrow with a cross on it, cut into the bed of a stone. Whoever put it there reckoned nobody'd ever see it. I'd say seventeen-hundreds, from the tooling.
A: Oh, that's lovely. It's like a signature, isn't it? Somebody's just saying, I was here. I think about that with the mill chimneys round me. There's one at the end of my road, the last one of about six, and every brick in it somebody laid by hand, and nobody knows their names, and I sort of draw it for them, I suppose. Sorry, that sounds daft.
B: Nah. It doesn't. That's exactly it.
A: My dad used to take me past them. He knew which mill was which. He's not here now, so.
B: Mine was the same with his. My grandad, really. Stories about the mills.
A: Do you draw them, mills?
B: Now and then. Mostly details. A doorway, a datestone. You should come over and draw Dean Clough. Big old carpet mill. Plenty of chimney.
A: I'd like that. I'd have to look up the buses.
B: Train to Halifax, then walk. Ten minutes.
A: Erm, did you want to do art, then? Like properly?
B: Teacher wanted me to go to art college. I didn't. Went for the apprenticeship.
A: I started a BTEC. Didn't finish it.
B: Doesn't stop you drawing.
A: No. I suppose not.
B: You can tell from that lock you look properly. That's the bit they can't teach you anyway.
A: Oh. Erm. Thank you. I don't know what to say to that.
B: Don't have to say owt.
A: Is that us, then?
